lead: TCP is the transport protocol behind web pages, email and file downloads. It turns the unreliable packet service of IP into a reliable, ordered stream of bytes between two processes. It does this with a connection, sequence numbers and acknowledgments. The 20-byte TCP header carries the two 32-bit numbers that make the whole thing work: the sequence number says which byte this segment starts at, and the acknowledgment number says which byte the receiver wants next. This chapter opens that header field by field.
prereq: You need chapter 5.1 for ports and the four-tuple, and chapter 5.2 for the checksum and pseudo-header.

blocks.text: TCP sits directly above IP. IP moves packets between hosts; TCP turns that into a connection between two processes, using the port numbers of chapter 5.1. The connection is identified by four values: source IP, source port, destination IP and destination port.

items: Connection-oriented. Both ends agree to talk before any data byte moves.
Reliable. Every byte is acknowledged; bytes that do not arrive are sent again.
Ordered byte stream. The receiver reads the same bytes in the same order. A write of 5000 bytes may arrive as three segments.
Full duplex. Data flows both ways at once; each direction has its own sequence numbers.
Flow control. The receiver advertises how much buffer space it has (chapter 5.5).
Congestion control. The sender probes the network and backs off when loss appears (chapter 5.6).

blocks.text: One connection carries one logical byte stream. TCP does not keep application message boundaries: if the program needs records, it must mark them itself.

sections.h3: Sequence numbers count bytes, not segments

blocks.text: TCP numbers every byte in the stream, not every segment. The two directions are numbered independently. Each side chooses an initial sequence number when it opens the connection (chapter 5.4). The SYN that opens the connection consumes one sequence number; after that, data bytes follow.

blocks.where: seq is the sequence number field of this segment; S₀ is the sequence number of the first data byte in this direction; B is the number of data bytes sent earlier in this connection.

blocks.text: The acknowledgment number is the next byte the receiver expects. It is cumulative: it confirms every byte below that number. If bytes 5000 to 7499 have arrived in order, the receiver sends acknowledgment number 7500. It does not send 7499.

blocks.where: ack is the acknowledgment number; S₀ is the sequence number of the first data byte; R is the number of data bytes received in order so far.

items: After both arrive, acknowledgment number is 7000.
SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number; their handling belongs to chapter 5.4.

blocks.text: Every TCP segment begins with a fixed 20-byte header. Options may add up to 40 bytes, so the header is 20 to 60 bytes. The fields are:

head: Field
Size
What it holds
rows: Number of the first data byte in this segment.
Next byte expected from the other direction.
Header length in 32-bit words; 5 means 20 bytes.
URG, ACK, PSH, RST, SYN, FIN, plus later CWR and ECE.
Receiver's advertised window for flow control.
Mandatory; covers header, data and pseudo-header (same as UDP).
Points to urgent data when URG is set.

blocks.text: The data offset counts 32-bit words, not bytes. A header of 24 bytes has data offset 6.

items: SYN starts a connection and FIN ends it.
ACK says the acknowledgment number is valid.
PSH asks the receiver to deliver data promptly.
URG marks urgent data; CWR and ECE support congestion notification.

blocks.text: Options carry MSS (maximum segment size, the largest TCP payload this side can receive), window scale, SACK permitted, and timestamp. If no MSS option is sent, the default MSS is 536 bytes. The option field is padded to a multiple of 4 bytes.

figure.caption: The two 32-bit numbers in the middle are the reliability mechanism; the window field on the fourth word is the flow-control mechanism of chapter 5.5.

examples.question: A TCP sender's first data byte is numbered 5000. It sends three segments carrying 1000, 1000 and 500 bytes of data. (a) Give the sequence number field of each segment. (b) Give the acknowledgment number the receiver returns after all three arrive in order. (c) Give the data offset value when the header carries a 4-byte MSS option.
steps: Segment 1 starts at byte 5000 and carries 1000 bytes, so its sequence number is 5000.
Acknowledgment number = 5000 + 2500 = 7500, the next byte expected.
Header length = 20-byte fixed part + 4-byte MSS option = 24 bytes.
examples.answer: The sequence numbers are 5000, 6000 and 7000; the acknowledgment number is 7500; the data offset is 6.
examples.check:
s0 = 5000
s1 = 1000
s2 = 1000
s3 = 500
seq1 = s0
seq2 = s0 + s1
seq3 = s0 + s1 + s2
ack = s0 + s1 + s2 + s3
header_bytes = 20 + 4
data_offset = header_bytes // 4
print(seq1)
print(seq2)
print(seq3)
print(ack)
print(data_offset)

traps: Counting segments instead of bytes: sequence numbers advance by the number of data bytes, not by one per segment.
Reading the acknowledgment number as the last byte received. It is the next byte expected, so it is one more than the last in-order byte.
Reading the data offset as bytes. It is in 32-bit words; 5 means 20 bytes, 6 means 24 bytes.
Confusing MSS with MTU. MSS is the largest TCP payload; MTU is the largest IP packet. The default MSS when no option is sent is 536 bytes.
Assuming TCP keeps message boundaries. A single application write can be split across segments, and one segment can carry bytes from two writes.

quiz.q: What does the acknowledgment number in a TCP header mean?
quiz.a: It is the next byte the receiver expects from the other direction. It is cumulative and confirms all bytes below that number.

quiz.q: How many bytes is the fixed TCP header, and what is the maximum header size with options?
quiz.a: The fixed header is 20 bytes. Options add up to 40 bytes, so the maximum is 60 bytes.

quiz.q: Why does TCP number bytes rather than segments?
quiz.a: TCP delivers an ordered byte stream, so it must identify every byte even when segment sizes change. Byte numbering lets the receiver acknowledge exactly how much arrived in order, place retransmitted bytes correctly, and reassemble the stream.

quiz.q: A TCP sender's first data byte is numbered 1200. It sends 300 bytes then 700 bytes in two segments. Give both sequence numbers and the acknowledgment number after both arrive in order.
quiz.a: First sequence number = 1200. Second sequence number = 1200 + 300 = 1500. Total data = 300 + 700 = 1000 bytes, so acknowledgment number = 1200 + 1000 = 2200.

quiz.q: A TCP header has 12 bytes of options. What is the data offset field?
quiz.a: Header size = 20 + 12 = 32 bytes. Data offset counts 32-bit words: 32 ÷ 4 = 8.

quiz.q: Segments carrying bytes 2000–2499 and 3000–3499 arrive; bytes 2500–2999 are lost. What acknowledgment number does the receiver send after each segment?
quiz.a: After the first segment the receiver sends 2500. After the second segment it still sends 2500, because the gap 2500–2999 has not arrived. The second acknowledgment is a duplicate ACK, which can trigger fast retransmit.

quiz.q: Why is the TCP checksum mandatory while the UDP checksum is optional in IPv4?
quiz.a: TCP promises reliable delivery, so a corrupted segment must be detected and discarded; the byte stream cannot contain undetected errors. A discarded segment is retransmitted. UDP does not promise reliability, so IPv4 allows the application to skip the checksum. The TCP checksum also covers the pseudo-header, which includes the IP addresses.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the window field in the TCP header?
quiz.a: The window field tells the sender how many bytes the receiver can accept beyond the acknowledgment number. It is the receiver's flow-control limit, so the sender must not have more unacknowledged bytes in flight than this window.

beyond: Not for the exam. In real stacks the TCP header is often compressed: a 20-byte header can shrink to a few bytes on a phone link, because most fields change little from packet to packet. Modern kernels also use TCP segmentation offload, so the header you read in a capture may be built by the network card, not the CPU. QUIC moves reliability and ordering into a new protocol above UDP, but it still carries the same ideas of sequence numbers, acknowledgments and windows. Search for TCP header options, window scaling, SACK, and TCP header compression.
